question: How does changing the scoring turn a return into a preparation?
intro: A low-string question and a repeated-note horn call frame a C-major fugato. When the scherzo returns, its weight has changed: quiet winds and plucked strings lead into the sustained bridge to the finale, not a self-contained ending.

sections.label: Scherzo return · reduced scoring
sections.mNote: quiet winds and pizzicato strings replace the earlier weight

cues.title: A question from below
cues.text: Cellos and double basses begin with a rising arpeggio. Quiet replies interrupt its upward motion, and fermatas loosen the three-beat pulse. The opening is not yet the repeated-note call that will dominate the louder passages.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf full score, printed p. 37, supplies the low-string arpeggio, replies and fermatas. The report’s opening alternates low relative-level windows; no individual release is timed.

cues.title: The horn rhythm
cues.text: The horn call uses three short attacks followed by a longer note, recalling the rhythm of the symphony’s opening movement. Its repeated pitches contrast with the low strings’ rising arpeggio: two different shapes organise the scherzo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf printed p. 37 gives the horn call after the two opening phrases. The report rises from −24.9 dB at 0:15 to −9.7 at 0:25, with its strongest boundary at 0:28. This locates the surrounding horn-call passage, not its first attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A scherzo without the name
cues.text: The score heads this movement simply “Allegro”, not “Scherzo”. Its fast triple metre and contrasting trio nevertheless preserve the outline of the symphonic dance movement. The familiar genre name describes its function rather than quoting Beethoven’s heading.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf printed p. 37 is headed Allegro; Eastman explains the scherzo designation and ternary design: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: The trio starts low
cues.text: The trio turns to C major and gives a running subject first to cellos and double basses. Other parts take it up in imitation. Follow the subject upwards through the ensemble rather than treating the low strings as accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf printed p. 42 shows the change to C major and low-string fugato, followed by successive entries. The report has a 1:26 boundary, a level drop after 1:20 and increased onset density during 1:25–1:45. The 1:26 trio start is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The third movement was revised
cues.text: The scherzo’s repeat scheme changed during the work’s early history. An extended five-part design and the shorter scherzo–trio–return design both belong to its performance tradition. This guide identifies the large contrasting spans without assigning every internal repeat.
cues.evidence: Eastman discusses the earlier five-part scheme and the shorter published design: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/. Internal repeat observance in this recording has not been established by score alignment or listening.

cues.title: Imitation changes the balance
cues.text: Within the fugato, keep track of which register carries the running subject. A new entry can become the foreground while an earlier entry continues underneath. The texture grows by overlapping lines rather than by adding a single tune above chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf printed pp. 42–46 shows the imitative trio. The report maintains relatively high attack density across 1:25–3:20, consistent with its active texture; the individual entries are not aligned.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A return without the blast
cues.text: The scherzo returns with much less weight. Plucked strings and quiet wind phrases replace the earlier force of the horn call. Recognise the rhythm through its changed attack: recurrence does not require restoring the original orchestration.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf printed pp. 46–49 writes the altered return, including pizzicato strings and quiet clarinet and bassoon phrases. The report’s 3:34 boundary is followed by a marked drop in brightness and relative level near −32 dB at 3:35. No single entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first and third conceived early
cues.text: The Fifth’s first and third movements were among its earliest-conceived material. Their shared short-short-short-long rhythm is therefore part of the work’s compositional history, not merely a connection imposed by later listeners.
cues.evidence: Eastman’s scherzo account, citing Lewis Lockwood, Beethoven’s Symphonies, p. 100, states that the first and third movements were the first conceived: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: An ending that waits
cues.text: The quiet return will not close with a full reprise and stop. Listen for the move from separated attacks towards sustained string notes and a persistent timpani pulse. The final span prepares another movement instead of completing this one in isolation.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf printed pp. 49–51 shows the return giving way to sustained strings, timpani and the attacca bridge. The report has a boundary at 4:58; this anticipatory cue does not place the first timpani stroke at 4:46.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Pressure gathers over the pulse
cues.text: Across the bridge’s final stretch, the sustained background and repeated pulse gather force. The violins rise and winds and brass join the final crescendo. The next movement supplies the C-major arrival; this file ends at the connecting boundary.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf printed pp. 50–52 connects the string–timpani bridge to the enlarged finale. The report rises from −29.1 dB at 5:15 to −20.4 at 5:30 and −10.2 in the final 5:35 window. Commons’ 2014 file history documents separating the finale from this file.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass becomes the subject
transitions.how: The repeated-note scherzo reaches its C-minor cadence and releases the heavier ensemble. The trio changes to C major and begins in cellos and double basses with running quavers. Bassoons and the remaining strings successively take up the subject. Triple metre continues, but chordal proclamation gives way to imitation: the lowest instruments are no longer merely supporting a theme elsewhere.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf printed p. 42 shows the cadence, C-major key signature and low-string subject with subsequent entries. The 1:26 boundary, level drop after 1:20 and higher onset density from 1:25 anchor the estimated trio start. Instrument entries are score-derived, not individually timed.

transitions.title: The same material loses its weight
transitions.how: The trio’s imitative movement thins and diminishes before the opening’s low-string shape returns in C minor. Beethoven rewrites the reprise: the repeated-note material passes into quiet winds and pizzicato strings rather than recovering the original horn-led force. The connection depends on familiar contour and rhythm surviving a change of attack and register. This altered return can continue into a bridge because it does not re-establish the opening’s full weight.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf printed pp. 45–47 supplies the diminishing trio and rewritten return. The report’s 3:34 boundary coincides with brightness falling from 987 Hz at 3:30 to 457 at 3:35 and lower relative level. The score’s return is placed broadly, not at a measured first note.

transitions.title: Sustained strings replace the detached replies
transitions.how: The detached replies give way to a sustained sonority: cellos and basses hold A♭ while first violins and violas hold C. Timpani repeat C beneath them. This is not yet the finale’s C-major chord; the A♭ in the bass keeps the harmony unsettled. The violin line then begins to move over the persistent background, and the crescendo prepares an uninterrupted passage into the finale.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf printed pp. 50–51 gives the A♭ bass, upper C and C-timpani pulse, then the growing bridge. The 4:58 boundary and reduced onset density around 5:00 support the change towards sustained writing; the first timpani attack is not aligned. Tonic pedal refers to the timpani’s C, not a C bass in the strings.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, III, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5
source.locator: Printed pp. 37–51. Broad passage map based on score and measured boundaries; internal repeat observance and individual entrances are not aligned.

timeline.note: Low strings begin the rising arpeggio; the reply comes from a different register.
Quiet orchestral replies interrupt the low-string question and lead towards another arpeggio.
The repeated-note horn call contrasts with the opening arpeggio; the full ensemble subsequently expands it.
The scherzo’s later forceful statements gather winds, brass and strings.
The C-major fugato starts at the bottom of the string ensemble.
Successive string and bassoon entries carry the running subject upwards.
Wind punctuation and imitative string lines share the trio’s later span.
The low-string question returns quietly before the rewritten, detached continuation.
Quiet winds exchange the repeated-note material with plucked and lightly bowed strings.
C in timpani and upper strings sounds against A♭ held by cellos and basses.
The violin line moves over the sustained lower strings and repeated timpani pulse.
Winds and brass join the bridge’s last crescendo; the finale’s extra instruments wait for the next movement.

composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
